thread.title: These 4 tech giants should make you think twice about this stock market

author: morningstar.com
title: These 4 tech giants should make you think twice about this stock market
text:
By Mark Hulbert, MarketWatch
Facebook, Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft dominate the S&P 500 -- and that's a problem
Measuring the stock market's valuation is made even more difficult than usual because of the dominant role currently played by a few giant technology companies.
Consider the four companies in the S&P 500 , other than Apple (AAPL) , with the largest market-caps currently -- Alphabet (a.k.a Google) (GOOGL) , Amazon.(AMZN) Microsoft (MSFT) and Facebook (FB) . The average P/E ratio of these four, based on trailing 12 months earnings, is 101.7 -- versus 25.6 for the S&P 500. If we focus on projected earnings over the next 12 months, these four companies' average P/E is 57.2, compared to 17.6 for the S&P 500.
Because these four firms' market caps dominate cap-weighted indices such as the S&P 500, their sky-high P/Es have an outsized influence. If you eliminated these four from consideration, the S&P 500's P/E would drop nearly 10%.
It's hard to believe that just four firms can have this much of an impact of the S&P 500 as a whole. Accordingly, both investment professionals and individual investors cannot ignore their outsized impact in analyzing the market.
Opinion:Big Tech shake-up -- three stocks to buy and three to sell (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/big-tech-shake-up-three-stocks-to-buy-and-three-to-sell-2018-02-26)
One possible conclusion reached by many advisers: The stock market is not as overvalued as the overall numbers suggest. For example, Nicholas Colas and Jessica Rabe, co-founders of DataTrek Research, have described the market as having two stages: "Tech is expensive and getting more so as it outperforms, while everything else treads water or sees at best modest valuation gains."
"The rest of the S&P 500 [other than the tech sector] is not expensive by historical norms," they note. "It's only a fluke of index construction that makes it seem so."
Another interpretation of the data paints a less-favorable picture. It focuses on the stock market's increasing dominance over the years by a few large, fast-growing companies. Their outsized influence is not a mere quirk of how indexes such as the S&P 500 are constructed.
One consequence of this recent trend is that the stock market has become increasingly vulnerable to the fortunes of these few dominant companies. This week we saw a hint of this: On Monday, Mar. 19, when Facebook's stock dropped (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/stocks-end-sharply-lower-as-facebook-tumbles-dow-negative-for-2018-2018-03-19) some 7%, the rest of the market plunged too, with the shedding more than 300 points.
How much do these few largest companies dominate the stock market of today? Consider the percentage of all corporate profits that come from the top 100 firms. In 1975 that percentage was 48.5%, according to research (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2869301)conducted by finance professors Kathleen Kahle of the University of Arizona and Rene Stulz of Ohio State. By 1995, 20 years later, it was only slightly higher, at 52.8%. But over the subsequent 20 years it skyrocketed and by 2015 stood at an amazing 84.2%.
Read: The 'popularity' stock ratio that warns tech's time may be up (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/the-popularity-stock-ratio-that-warns-techs-time-may-be-up-2018-03-20)
In other words, we now live in an economy in which all but 100 of the nearly 4,000 publicly traded corporations are scrambling for the few crumbs left after the mega-earners have eaten. Some have referred to this situation as a "winner take all economy (https://www.wsj.com/articles/investing-in-a-winner-takes-all-economy-1491790561)," and predict that these top earners will come to dominate the stock market even more.
If so, then investors need to rethink how to gauge the market's overall valuation. There would be little solace in knowing that the majority of companies are not overvalued, since it's the mega-caps' valuation that really matters.
That in turn means that today's stock market is especially vulnerable to even a small earnings misstep at any of these mega-cap companies. Watch out.
